The MeshCore TCP link is UNENCRYPTED and UNAUTHENTICATED.

• Every message you send or receive crosses the network in plain text.
• Repeater and room passwords cross the network in plain text.
• Anyone who can reach the radio's IP and port can control your radio.

Only use TCP to reach a Wi-Fi or Ethernet MeshCore node on a trusted network you control, never over untrusted Wi-Fi or the open internet.

The code contains the channel\'s secret key. Anyone who scans it can read everything on this channel, including messages sent before they scanned, because the key never changes and the cipher has no forward secrecy.\n\nThere\'s no way to revoke it: undoing a share means changing the key on every device that uses the channel.
Anyone who scans this can read the channel. Show it only to people you mean to give that to.
This node announced %1$s when it was told to update, so it can be identified exactly.
No update-mode address was recorded for this node, so it will be identified by what it advertises, and named before anything is written to it.

A node in update mode is off the mesh and can only be reached over Bluetooth, from within range of it.\n\n\"Restart it\" asks its bootloader to boot the firmware it already has. That works when the transfer never got as far as erasing anything, the usual case for an update that failed early. If the firmware was already erased, it depends on the bootloader: OTAFIX comes back in update mode, ready to be flashed again, but the standard bootloader comes back as a USB drive and stops answering over Bluetooth. On a standard bootloader, don\'t use this on a node whose transfer had started.

The radio will use %1$s from now on.

• It keeps pairing with the OLD PIN until the node restarts: the firmware picks the active PIN at startup. You'll be offered a reboot.
• This phone is already paired with the OLD PIN, and only Android can drop that pairing ("Forget device" in the system Bluetooth settings, not Remove under saved radios here). Until you do, the phone reconnects on the old pairing and the change looks like it did nothing.
• Every other phone paired with this radio has to do the same.
• Nothing can read the PIN back off the radio. If you forget it, Bluetooth access is gone until you reach the node another way: USB, or a factory reset that takes its identity with it.

Write it down before you continue.

The new PIN is stored, but the radio keeps pairing with the old one until it restarts.\n\nAfter the reboot your phone will still reconnect without asking for the new PIN: Android remembers the old pairing and only Android can drop it. To test the PIN, remove the pairing in the system Bluetooth settings (\"Forget device\"), which is NOT the same as Remove under saved radios here.

Android is holding a pairing made with the OLD PIN, and an app can\'t delete it. Radios without GPS lose their clock when they power-cycle. Drift matters beyond timestamps: message order and reaction matching both use the sender\'s clock, so a skewed radio makes other apps attach your reactions to the wrong message.

A message that fails twice is retried once as a flood.

MeshCore\'s documented default. If a repeater your path went through goes away, retrying that path can\'t work, so the third attempt clears the stored path and floods, which also lets the reply teach your radio a working route. With this off, a stale path keeps failing until something else refreshes it. It\'s capped at one flood per message.

The radio isn\'t adding repeaters. This app can add the useful ones:
\"Relayed\" means 3 or more messages in the last week.

A message\'s route lists a short hash for each repeater it went through. A repeater counts as relaying your traffic when its hash appears in the routes of at least 3 messages you received in the last week; fewer could be a one-off flood from far away, or another node sharing the hash. When another node you know shares the same short hash, the relays could be the other one\'s, so that repeater isn\'t counted.
Favourites are never overwritten. \"Oldest\" is the node heard from least recently.

Sends raw bytes to a channel. Nothing in this app reads them.

A datagram names an application by its 16-bit data type, not a person; see the firmware\'s docs/number_allocations.md. FF00–FFFF needs no registration and is the range to test with. Received datagrams appear in the diagnostics log with their type and payload in hex; they\'re never shown as text, because the bytes belong to another application and are chosen by whoever sent them.\n\nChange the payload every time. A datagram has no timestamp, so the same type and payload make an identical packet, and the mesh drops it as already seen. It still says \"Sent\" (the radio did transmit it), but nothing receives it.
The payload must be an even number of hex digits.
Refused. Check the channel exists, the type isn\'t 0000 and the payload is 1–163 bytes.

Restart the node now to apply it
A node never answers a reboot: the firmware restarts before it can reply, and sends no acknowledgement. Silence here is what success looks like.
A rebooted node announces itself only to radios in direct range, and its next flooded advert can be 47 hours away. So the new identity is written here, not waited for.
Asking the node what board it is…

Two steps, and only the first goes over the mesh.

1. `start ota` turns the node's Bluetooth on and makes it advertise for an update. It keeps running and repeating; nothing reboots yet, and the command can stay sent until you get there.
2. The firmware itself is carried over Bluetooth, from a phone next to the node. There's no way to do this over LoRa. Connecting is what reboots it into its bootloader.
Before you send this to a node you can\'t reach

Sending the command is safe: the node carries on repeating with its Bluetooth on, and a node nobody ever reaches is still doing its job. Rebooting it costs a reboot\'s downtime, nothing more.\n\nThe point of no return is later, when the transfer starts. Most stock bootloaders erase the application first, so a node interrupted after that has nothing to fall back to and waits in update mode until someone flashes it again. The OTAFIX bootloader recovers into update mode by itself, and is worth putting on over USB before a node goes up anywhere awkward.

Nodes on masts and roofs can\'t be approached, and this is the signal they have. A weak link often carries a whole image anyway: the transfer is slow rather than doomed.\n\nWhat it costs when it doesn\'t finish depends on the bootloader. The old firmware is erased as the transfer begins. The OTAFIX bootloader then waits in update mode for another attempt; the standard one won\'t start another over Bluetooth, and finishing needs a USB cable.

What can be updated over the air

Over-the-air updates need an nRF52 board running companion firmware v1.15 or newer, connected over Bluetooth; that\'s where the update service lives.\n\nESP32 boards (Heltec V3 and similar) update over USB, or over their own WiFi hotspot after `start ota`: connect to \"MeshCore OTA\" and open http://192.168.4.1/update in a browser. That path is deliberately not built into this app: a browser does it properly, and this app doesn\'t use WiFi.
You have to be within Bluetooth range; this doesn\'t go over the mesh.

A node that has taken `start ota` is still running its own firmware and still repeating; it has just turned its Bluetooth on and is advertising for an update.\n\nIt reboots into its bootloader when this app connects and starts the transfer, not before. Until then nothing is committed, and walking away costs nothing.
Before updating a node you can\'t easily reach

A failed transfer leaves the node in update mode, waiting, not bricked. It can be flashed again from close by. What it can\'t do is go back to running MeshCore on its own.\n\nThe stock bootloader on most boards erases flash before it starts, so a node interrupted mid-update has no application to fall back on. The OTAFIX bootloader (github.com/oltaco/Adafruit_nRF52_Bootloader_OTAFIX) returns to update mode by itself when that happens, and is strongly recommended before updating anything on a mast.

Off-grid encrypted LoRa messaging for MeshCore radios. No servers, no accounts, no Google Play Services, no analytics, no crash reporting.
MeshConnect is a fork of MeshCore Hardened. Its protocol layer, engine, storage and most screens are their work.
Transports, foreground service and app scaffolding, by the same author
The mesh firmware and protocol this app speaks
Map tiles and firmware downloads are the only internet connections, and both can be avoided.
Messages, contacts and keys live on this phone and the radio. Nothing is uploaded.
Channels are obfuscated, not secure: AES-ECB with a 2-byte MAC, and the key never changes.
Advert signatures are verified before a contact is imported.
Secrets sit in the device keystore and the message database is encrypted.
